prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I’m jotting down these lines, having borrowed a pen from a waitress in this roadside restaurant. Three rusty pines prop up the sky in the windows. My soup gets cold, which implies I’ll eat it cold. Soon I too will leave a tip on the table, merge into the beehive of travelers and board one of the ferries, where there’s always a line to the loo and no one knows where the captain is. Slightly seasick, I keep on writing of the wind-rose and lobster traps, seagulls, if any—and there always are. Check the air and you’ll see them above straw hats and caps. The sun at noon glides like a monstrous star- fish through clouds. Others drink iced tea, training binoculars on a tugboat. When I finish this letter, I’ll take a gulp from the flask you gave me for the road in days when I was too young to care about those on the pier who waved goodbye. I miss them now: cousins in linen dresses, my mother, you, boys in light summer shirts. Life is too long. The compass needle dances. Everything passes by. The ferry passes by ragged yellow shores.

outputs.L2:
I’m scribbling this with a pen lent to me by a server at a roadside diner. Through the windows, three weathered pine trees seem to hold up the heavens. My soup is cooling, so I suppose I’ll have it cold. Before long, I’ll leave some money on the table, join the swarm of people in transit, and step aboard a ferry, where the restroom always has a queue and the captain is nowhere to be found.

Though a little nauseated by the motion, I continue writing about the compass rose, lobster pots, and whatever gulls may be around—and gulls are invariably there. Look upward and you’ll spot them circling over straw hats and caps. At midday, the sun moves through the clouds like an enormous starfish. Other passengers sip iced tea and aim their binoculars at a tugboat.

Once this letter is done, I’ll drink from the flask you gave me for the journey, back when I was too young to think much about the people standing on the dock and waving farewell. Now I long for them: my cousins in their linen dresses, my mother, you, and the boys wearing pale summer shirts. Life goes on for too long. The compass needle quivers and spins. Everything slips past. The ferry moves alongside frayed, yellow-colored shores.
outputs.L3:
The narrator sits writing in a roadside restaurant, where a bowl of soup has grown cold. Beyond the window, the surrounding landscape seems suspended in stillness, creating a brief pause in the larger journey. Yet this quiet is temporary. Soon, the narrator will join the other travelers boarding a crowded ferry, a place of confusion and constant movement, where passengers struggle with luggage, shifting decks, and seasickness.

As the ferry moves along the coast, the narrator’s attention turns to vivid details: lobster traps stacked near the water, seagulls circling overhead, clouds gathering and dispersing across the sky, and a tugboat working steadily in the harbor. These images give the journey a sharp physical presence while also reflecting its restless, uncertain mood.

Among the narrator’s belongings is an old flask, an object that connects the present voyage with the past. It recalls earlier departures and the loved ones who once stood on the pier, waving goodbye as the distance between them widened. Their remembered gestures transform the crossing into more than a simple trip. The journey becomes a meditation on longing, memory, and the passage of time. As land and sea continually shift around the ferry, the narrator is reminded that life itself is unstable: people leave, moments vanish, and every pause eventually gives way to motion.
outputs.L4:
I am writing from a roadside restaurant near the ferry landing, where trucks idle in the gravel yard and the windows tremble whenever one of them pulls away. The room smells of coffee, frying oil, and wet coats. Outside, rain has darkened the road and polished the roofs of the waiting cars. Beyond them, half obscured by mist, the ferry moves toward us with the grave patience of an old animal.

From here it seems less like a vessel than a loose piece of the shore, carrying its lamps and iron rails across the gray water. Gulls turn above it, bright scraps of paper caught in the wind. When the doors open, cars pour out in a slow procession, shining with rain, and for a moment the landing becomes a small, confused city of headlights, shouted instructions, and engines. Then the commotion passes. The ferry takes on another cargo of strangers, and I go with them.

On deck, the wind is sharper than it appeared from land. It pulls at collars, flattens hair, and sends passengers retreating behind the glass. I remain outside. The wake spreads behind us in two white roads that widen and vanish. Islands drift past, dark-backed and silent, like whales sleeping just beneath the surface. Along the distant coast, houses appear one by one and then disappear into the fog before I can imagine the lives within them.

Travel makes everything seem both near and unreachable. A light on shore may be only a mile away, yet the water between us gives it the distance of a star. I think of the people I once left standing in doorways and railway stations, their faces composed for farewell. At the time, departure seemed simple: one lifted a bag, boarded a train or ship, and trusted that affection would remain where it had been placed. I believed memory was a room that could be returned to unchanged.

Now I know that rooms are altered by absence. Chairs are moved. Photographs fade. Voices acquire unfamiliar pauses. Even those who wait are carried forward by a current invisible to the one who has gone. We say we have left people behind, but no one stays behind. Each of us is borne away on a separate tide.

The ferry sounds its horn. The note rolls over the water, immense and lonely, and for an instant it seems to call not only to the harbor ahead but to every shore already lost. I remember hands raised in farewell, letters begun and abandoned, names I have not spoken for years. Their absence does not diminish with distance; it gathers weight. The farther I travel, the more crowded the journey becomes.

Dusk settles early. Reflections rise in the cabin windows, laying the pale faces of passengers over the darkening sea. We sit together without speaking, each carrying a private country. A child sleeps against his mother’s shoulder. An old man watches the wake until it is swallowed by night. Cups slide faintly on the tables as the ship turns.

Life is longer than we imagine when we are young, and less certain. Its crossings multiply. One shore recedes before the next becomes clear, and much of the voyage is spent between them, surrounded by weather and moving water. We believe we are traveling toward something permanent, but every arrival contains the first small motion of departure.

Soon the lamps of the farther harbor appear. People gather their coats and luggage. Engines start below us, and the deck vibrates underfoot. I close my notebook and look back once more, though there is nothing to see now but darkness, the broken foam of our passage, and a few distant lights wavering at the edge of the world.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical prose poem in the form of a letter composed at a roadside restaurant before boarding a ferry, filled with maritime imagery, nostalgia, and reflections on time passing.
counterfactuals.output:
Dear Mira,

I am writing from a roadside restaurant where the windows tremble whenever a truck passes, and the salt shakers stand like two small lighthouses beside my cup. Beyond the parking lot, the road descends toward the harbor. I can see the ferry waiting there, white and patient, breathing smoke into the afternoon.

The waitress has brought me coffee in a chipped blue mug. It tastes faintly of tin and old weather. Around me, spoons ring against bowls, strangers lean over their meals, and the clock above the kitchen advances with the stubbornness of a tide. In forty minutes they will lift the gangway. In forty minutes the town will loosen its hold on me, and the water will begin translating everything into distance.

Do you remember the summer we crossed this channel together? We stood at the rail while gulls followed in our wake, their wings flashing like torn letters. You said the islands looked like sleeping animals. I pretended not to be cold. We believed then that time was a country we could leave whenever we wished, that years were only buoys marking a route back home.

Now the harbor is full of rust and ropes. The boats knock softly against the pier, each one repeating the same unfinished sentence. Even the sea seems older, though perhaps it is only I who have learned to see age everywhere: in the gray boards of the dock, in the waitress’s hands, in my own reflection floating over the glass like a face beneath water.

Soon I will pay, fold this letter, and carry it aboard. The ferry horn will sound across the bay—a great animal calling through fog—and the shore will begin to diminish: restaurant, road, roofs, all drawn into the blue seam of evening. Somewhere behind me, our younger selves will remain at the rail, laughing into the wind, certain the crossing has no end.

If this reaches you, think of me between shores, with night gathering over the water and the engines turning below like enormous clocks. Think of the moon laying its pale road across the waves. I will follow it as long as I can, though every voyage leads away from something, and every wake closes almost as soon as it is made.

Yours, from the last table by the window.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a first-person travel vignette about someone writing with a borrowed pen while their soup grows cold, then joining other travelers on a ferry. Use surreal metaphors and end on a melancholy image of the shoreline.
counterfactuals.output:
I wrote with a borrowed pen while my soup grew cold beside me. The pen leaked blue moons onto my fingers, and every sentence seemed to loosen another nail from the afternoon. Across the café window, rain stitched the harbor to the sky. My spoon rested in the broth like a drowned compass.

When the ferry horn sounded, I closed the notebook and returned the pen to the waiter. He tucked it behind his ear, where it looked like a small, sleeping oar.

At the pier, I joined the other travelers beneath their umbrellas. We filed aboard carrying suitcases, flowers, cages of private weather. The engines woke under our feet, a pair of iron animals dreaming of distance. Soon the town slipped backward, its roofs folding into one another like tired red wings.

No one spoke. Gulls circled above us, torn scraps from an unanswered letter. I stood at the rail, my ink-stained hand growing numb in the wind, and watched the shoreline diminish into a thin gray scar the sea could not quite heal.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poetic monologue that includes three pine trees, a crowded ferry, seagulls, lobster traps, iced tea, binoculars, a flask given by a loved one, and memories of family waving goodbye.
counterfactuals.output:
Three pine trees stand at the edge of the harbor,  
shoulder to shoulder, dark as old sentinels,  
their needles stitching the wind to the sky.

Below them, a crowded ferry pulls away—  
decks bright with strangers, coats and restless hands,  
while seagulls wheel above the wake, crying  
as if departure were a wound they understood.

Along the dock, lobster traps lie stacked  
like small, weathered rooms no one can enter.  
I sit beside them with my iced tea sweating  
in the brief, salt-heavy warmth, binoculars  
resting in my lap.

In my pocket is the flask you gave me,  
silver dulled by years and the touch of my thumb.  
I do not drink. I only hold it,  
as though your hand might still be wrapped around it,  
as though love were a warmth metal could remember.

Through the binoculars, faces sharpen, then blur.  
For a moment I see my family again—  
all of you at the rail, waving goodbye,  
your arms rising and falling against the distance  
until you became white sleeves, then specks, then nothing.

Still, I wave.

The ferry grows smaller.  
The seagulls turn inland.  
The three pine trees keep their silence.

And I remain on the shore,  
holding what was given, watching what is gone,  
while the sea carries every farewell  
farther than the eye can follow.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a wistful, slightly absurdist prose passage narrated by a seasick traveler addressing someone from their past. Emphasize transience, regret, and the belated realization that farewells matter.
counterfactuals.output:
You would have laughed at me now, leaning over the rail as if the sea had asked a question only my stomach could answer. The gulls follow with bureaucratic patience. One of them has been beside us since dawn, or else several gulls have agreed to impersonate the same regret.

I did not say goodbye properly. That is the trouble. I thought departures were only doors behaving dramatically, and that every road, train, ship, or winter would eventually grow embarrassed and return what it had taken. So I waved with one hand while searching my pocket with the other. I said, “See you,” as though seeing were inevitable.

Now the coast has thinned to a pencil mark, then to a rumor. My suitcase slides back and forth across the cabin, practicing its own small migration. Inside it are three shirts, a broken comb, and the blue cup you hated. I brought the cup by accident. Or perhaps objects understand farewells better than we do and arrange their own escapes.

The ship keeps rising, falling, rising—an indecisive god. Between heaves, I remember your face at the station: how you waited for me to add something, anything, to the ordinary words. I had whole countries of feeling then, but no customs declaration.

If I could return, I would not promise to stay. We both know what promises become: pale furniture in abandoned rooms. I would only stand still. I would look at you long enough to admit that the moment was leaving us.

The gull has vanished. The coast is gone. Even my nausea feels temporary, which is almost insulting.

Goodbye, then—late, salt-stained, and addressed to no shore I can see.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a literary prose poem about departure and memory, beginning in a roadside restaurant and moving onto a ferry. Include the lines “Life is too long,” “The compass needle dances,” and “Everything passes by.”
counterfactuals.output:
In the roadside restaurant, the tables wore thin skins of sunlight, and the waitress poured coffee as if filling small graves. Trucks sighed beyond the windows. Your coat hung from the chair beside me, though you had already left, and for a moment memory seemed no more than fabric keeping the shape of a body.

“Life is too long,” you once said, breaking bread with both hands. I laughed then. Now the words return with the taste of salt and burnt sugar.

By dusk I am on the ferry. The harbor loosens its ropes; gulls wheel like scraps of torn letters. Cars sleep below deck, carrying suitcases, flowers, tools, the secret weight of other lives. On the blackening water, the wake opens and closes behind us.

“The compass needle dances,” says the sailor, tapping the glass. As if direction were joy. As if trembling meant we had not lost our way.

The shore diminishes: restaurant, road, last window lit against the hills. I hold your absence like a ticket gone soft in my palm. The ferry enters fog, and even the stars withdraw their names.

“Everything passes by.”

Yet in the passing, something remains: the cup cooling between us, your sleeve brushing mine, the road going on without witness. Memory is not an anchor. It is the water remembering, for one bright instant, the shape of the ship.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
